docs.title: What is an Activity Definition?
docs.heading_path: Activity Definition > What is an Activity Definition?
docs.snippet: An Activity Definition is the code that defines the constraints of an Activity Task Execution. Activities encapsulate business logic that is prone to failure, allowing for automatic retries when issues occur.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.heading_path: Activity Definition > What is an Activity Definition? > Idempotency
docs.snippet: Idempotence means that performing an operation multiple times has the same result as performing it once. In the context of Temporal, Activities should be designed to be safely executed multiple times without causing unexpected or undesired side effects.

docs.snippet: - **Pausing an Activity doesn't affect the parent Workflow.** The Workflow continues Running, and  Signals, Queries, and Updates on the parent Workflow are unaffected. - **No further retries are scheduled.** The Temporal Service stops scheduling retries. This is enforced…

docs.snippet: - The downstream service or dependency that caused you to Pause has recovered. - A code deploy or configuration change is complete and the Activity is safe to retry. - You Paused an Activity for investigation and are ready to let it proceed.

docs.title: What happens when you Unpause an Activity
docs.heading_path: Activity Operations > Unpause > What happens when you Unpause an Activity

docs.title: Important considerations
docs.heading_path: Activity Operations > Unpause > Important considerations
docs.snippet: - **Unpausing many Activities at once can overwhelm downstream services.** If you Paused multiple Activities because a  service was down, Unpausing them all at the same time sends all retries simultaneously. Consider Unpausing in batches  to avoid overwhelming a recovering…

docs.title: Observability
docs.heading_path: Reset retry state but don't resume yet > Observability
docs.snippet: Activity Operations have a limited audit trail because they are not recorded in a Workflow's Event History. However, you can use the CLI and the UI to check Activity state and find Paused Activities for running Workflows.

docs.title: Check Activity state
docs.heading_path: Reset retry state but don't resume yet > Observability > Check Activity state
docs.snippet: temporal workflow describe shows the current state of each pending Activity, including whether it's Paused, its current attempt count, and last failure. The UI shows who performed an operation, when, and why (if a --reason was provided).

docs.title: Find Paused Activities
docs.heading_path: Reset retry state but don't resume yet > Observability > Find Paused Activities
docs.snippet: There's no Namespace-wide query to find all Paused Activities across Workflows. You must know the Workflow Id.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.heading_path: Reset retry state but don't resume yet > Observability > Audit trail
docs.snippet: Activity Operations don't produce Event History events. There is no record of a Pause, Reset, or option change in the Workflow's Event History. Nothing that reads the Event History - Workflow code, Replays, or external tooling - will see that an Operation occurred.

docs.title: What is a Local Activity?

docs.snippet: A Local Activity is an Activity Execution that executes in the same Worker process as the Workflow Execution that schedules it.

docs.title: How Local Activities execute
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > How Local Activities execute
docs.snippet: 1. A Workflow schedules an Activity. 2. The Workflow completes its Workflow Task by sending a ScheduleActivityTask command to the Temporal Service. 3. The Temporal Service creates an Activity Task. 4. An Activity Worker polls the Activity Task Queue and executes the Activity. 5.…

docs.title: Workflow Task heartbeating
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > Workflow Task heartbeating
docs.snippet: Local Activities do **not** support Activity heartbeats. Instead, the SDK supports Workflow Task heartbeating.

docs.title: Failure and durability
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > Failure and durability
docs.snippet: Regular Activities are durably tracked by the Temporal Service. Scheduling, completion, retries, and failures are all recorded in the Event history. If a Worker crashes after an Activity completes, the completed Activity is not executed again.

docs.title: Mixing Local Activities and regular Activities
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > Mixing Local Activities and regular Activities

docs.title: Choosing between regular Activities and Local Activities
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > Choosing between regular Activities and Local Activities
docs.snippet: Choose a regular Activity unless you have a specific need for the performance optimization that Local Activities provide.

docs.title: Use cases for Local Activities
docs.heading_path: Local Activity > Choosing between regular Activities and Local Activities > Use cases for Local Activities
docs.snippet: - Lightweight data transformations - Small computations - Reading from an in-memory cache - Fast local filesystem operations - High-throughput Workflows with many very short-lived operations

docs.title: What is a Standalone Activity?
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > What is a Standalone Activity?
docs.snippet: If you need to orchestrate multiple Activities, use a Workflow. But if you just need to execute a single Activity, use a Standalone Activity.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > Use cases
docs.snippet: Standalone Activities can be used for durable job processing use cases such as sending an email, processing a webhook, syncing data, or executing a single function reliably with built-in retries and timeouts.

docs.title: Key features
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > Key features
docs.snippet: Key features - Execute any Temporal Activity as a top-level primitive without the overhead of a Workflow - Native async job processing model: schedule -> dispatch -> process -> result - No head-of-line blocking - a slow job doesn’t block the dispatch of other Tasks - Arbitrary…

docs.title: Observability
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > Observability
docs.snippet: All existing Activity metrics apply to Standalone Activities. This includes counts for scheduled, started, completed, failed, timed out, and canceled activities.

docs.title: Public Preview limitations
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > Public Preview limitations
docs.snippet: - Pause, reset, and update options are not supported in Public Preview but scheduled for GA. - TerminateExisting conflict policy / TerminateIfRunning reuse policy is not supported yet.

docs.title: Temporal CLI support
docs.heading_path: Standalone Activity > Temporal CLI support
docs.snippet: Standalone Activities require Temporal CLI v1.7.0 or higher and Temporal Server v1.31.0 or higher.

docs.snippet: A Worker is the application component responsible for running your Workflow and Activity code, built with a Temporal SDK. Workers have historically been long-running processes deployed on bare metal, virtual machines, or in containers.

docs.title: Client application

docs.snippet: Temporal Clients offer a set of APIs to communicate with a Temporal Service. They are one aspect of your Temporal application and provided by a Temporal SDK. You instantiate and use it in your own application code to start and manage Workflow Executions.

docs.title: The Temporal Server
docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server
docs.snippet: The Temporal Server is the heart of the platform. It's responsible for orchestrating Workflow Execution, maintaining state, and ensuring reliability.

docs.title: Frontend Service
docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server > Frontend Service
docs.snippet: From your application's perspective, the Frontend Service is the Temporal endpoint your Temporal Client talks to. Your client sends requests (start Workflow, Signal, Query, etc.) to the Frontend, and the Frontend forwards them to the appropriate backend services.

docs.title: Temporal Service backend
docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server > Temporal Service backend
docs.snippet: The backend consists of several specialized services including the History, Matching, and Worker services, and a Persistence Layer.

docs.title: History Service
docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server > Temporal Service backend > History Service
docs.snippet: The History Service is the part of Temporal that keeps track of everything that happens in each Workflow. It writes an ordered Event History to the database so Temporal always knows what has happened. This includes when a Workflow started, Activities ran, Signals were received,…

docs.title: Matching Service
docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server > Temporal Service backend > Matching Service
docs.snippet: The Matching Service manages most of the coordination with the other services, especially the Task Queues or Task Queue partitions. This is where Tasks are dispatched to their respective queues before being picked up by the corresponding Workers. To determine how many more Tasks…

docs.heading_path: Temporal architecture > The Temporal Server > Temporal Service backend > Worker Service
docs.snippet: The Worker Service is where all of the background functionality that keeps the Temporal Service running smoothly is handled. It takes care of all the internal/system Workflows that Temporal needs like maintenance jobs, cleanup, replication, archival, and visibility indexing. You…
